topic: The Inseparable Duo: The Inverse Relationship Between Derivatives and Integrals
target_audience: High school seniors or first-year university students

outline.topic: The Inseparable Duo: The Inverse Relationship Between Derivatives and Integrals
outline.target_audience: High school seniors or first-year university students

sections.title: The Cheetah's Journey: Speed vs. Distance
sections.content: Introduce the big picture through a real-world scenario. Explain that motion can be viewed in two ways: how fast you are going at an instant (Derivative) and how much ground you've covered in total (Integral).
sections.example: An animation of a Cheetah running. A 'Speedometer' shows its instantaneous velocity (Derivative), while an 'Odometer' tracks its total displacement (Integral). The goal is to show that if you know one, you can find the other.

sections.title: Prerequisite Recap: Slope and Area
sections.content: Briefly revisit the graphical meaning of both concepts to build a foundation. Define the Derivative as the 'Slope' of a tangent line and the Definite Integral as the 'Area' under a curve.
sections.example: A split-screen visual: On the left, a line touching a curve at one point (Slope/Rate). On the right, the region under a curve filled with color (Area/Accumulation).

sections.title: The Accumulation Function
sections.content: Introduce a 'growing' area. If we have a function f(t), let's define a new function A(x) that calculates the area from a fixed start point to a moving point 'x'. This is the 'Area Function'.
sections.example: A graph of a curve where a vertical 'curtain' moves from left to right. As the curtain moves, the shaded area increases. This changing area is represented by a new growing graph below it.

sections.title: The Core Insight: How Fast Does Area Grow?
sections.content: Ask the critical question: At what rate is the shaded area increasing at any moment 'x'? Demonstrate visually that the 'extra slice' of area added is proportional to the height of the original function f(x).
sections.example: Zoom into the edge of the moving 'curtain' from Section 3. Show a tiny sliver of width 'dx'. The area added is approximately f(x) times dx. Therefore, the rate of change of Area (dA/dx) is exactly the height of the curve f(x).

sections.title: The Fundamental Theorem: Two Sides of a Coin
sections.content: Synthesize the observation: Differentiation and Integration are inverse operations. If you integrate a function to get the area, and then differentiate that area, you get the original function back.
sections.example: A 'Mathematical Loop' animation: Start with f(x) -> Integrate -> Get Area Function F(x) -> Differentiate -> Return to f(x). Use the analogy of a 'climbing' robot (Integration) and its 'downhill' speed sensor (Differentiation).

sections.title: Application: The Power of the Relationship
sections.content: Explain why this matters: We can find areas without drawing thousands of tiny rectangles. We just need to find the 'Anti-derivative'.
sections.example: Calculating the area under a parabola y=x². Instead of counting blocks, we find its anti-derivative (x³/3), plug in the endpoints, and get the exact area instantly. The Cheetah's total distance is simply the 'anti-derivative' of its speed function.

storyboard.title: The Cheetah's Journey: Speed vs. Distance
lecture_lines: Meet our cheetah racing across the savanna.
Speedometer shows its instantaneous speed, the derivative.
Odometer tracks total distance covered, the integral.
animations: Fade in a Cheetah silhouette (#D4AF37) moving across the screen.
Display a circular Speedometer (#FFFFFF) with a needle fluctuating.
Show an Odometer (#FFFFFF) with digits increasing as Cheetah moves.
Highlight the Speedometer; label it "Derivative of Distance" (#00FFFF).
Highlight the Odometer; label it "Integral of Speed" (#FFD700).

storyboard.title: Prerequisite Recap: Slope and Area
lecture_lines: Recall that derivatives represent the slope of curves.
In contrast, integrals represent the area under curves.
We will now link these two fundamental concepts.
animations: Draw a green curve (#00FF00); animate a magenta tangent line (#FF00FF) sliding along it.
Shade the area under a different part of the green curve (#00FF00) in light green.
Display labels "Slope (Rate)" and "Area (Accumulation)" in white (#FFFFFF) on opposite sides.

storyboard.title: The Accumulation Function
lecture_lines: Imagine a moving curtain sweeping across a graph.
Shaded area grows as the curtain moves right.
This growing area defines the accumulation function.
As input x increases, the total area accumulates.
This function maps points to their total area.
animations: Draw a green curve f(t) (#00FF00); show a vertical white line (#FFFFFF) at t=0.
Move the vertical line to the right to x; shade the area A(x) (#00FF00) as it moves.
Simultaneously plot a new orange curve A(x) (#FF8C00) below, representing the total area.

storyboard.title: The Core Insight: How Fast Does Area Grow?
lecture_lines: How fast does this accumulated area actually grow?
Consider a tiny sliver added at position x.
The sliver height is exactly the function's height.
Area added equals height times the tiny width.
The growth rate is the original function's height.
animations: Zoom into the edge of the shaded area at x; show a thin rectangle (#FFFF00) of width dx.
Label the height of the rectangle f(x) (#00FF00) and the width dx (#FFFFFF).
Show the formula dA = f(x) * dx in yellow (#FFFF00).
Rearrange the formula to dA/dx = f(x) with a transform animation.
Highlight the result: the slope of A(x) is f(x).

storyboard.title: The Fundamental Theorem: Two Sides of a Coin
lecture_lines: The area's derivative is the original function's height.
Differentiation and integration are inverse operations.
Integrating a rate gives you the total accumulation.
Differentiating accumulation returns the original rate.
They are two sides of the same coin.
animations: Place f(x) (#00FF00) at the top; draw a clockwise arrow labeled "Integrate" (#00FFFF).
The arrow leads to F(x) (#FF8C00) at the bottom.
Draw another clockwise arrow labeled "Differentiate" (#FF00FF) from F(x) back to f(x).
Flash the entire loop in white (#FFFFFF) to emphasize the cycle.
Display the text "Fundamental Theorem of Calculus" (#FFFFFF) in the center of the loop.

storyboard.title: Application: The Power of the Relationship
lecture_lines: This relationship lets us calculate areas with ease.
Find the anti-derivative to solve complex integrals.
Total distance is simply the anti-derivative of speed.
animations: Plot y=x^2 (#00FF00); shade the area from x=0 to x=2.
Display the anti-derivative F(x) = x^3/3 (#FFFFFF) next to the graph.
Calculate F(2) - F(0) = 8/3; update the area label to "8/3" (#FFFF00).
